title: Weiqi Overview
audience: Readers who want a first structural map of weiqi before studying joseki, life and death, or advanced strategy.
learningGoal: Explain how {{liberty}}, {{capture}}, {{territory}}, and {{ko}} organize play in weiqi.

steps.title: An empty board
steps.text: Imagine an empty 9 by 9 board. Weiqi is played by placing black and white stones on the grid's intersections, not its squares.

steps.title: Black plays the first stone
steps.text: Black places one stone near the center. A stone in open space like this has four {{liberty:liberties}} -- the empty points directly adjacent to it.

steps.title: White approaches
steps.text: White places a stone on one of the four intersections adjacent to Black's stone. Black's group is down to three {{liberty:liberties}}.

steps.title: White surrounds a second side
steps.text: White plays a second adjacent stone. Two {{liberty:liberties}} remain.

steps.title: Atari
steps.text: White plays a third adjacent stone. Black's stone now has only one remaining liberty, at E6 -- it is in {{atari}}, the game's simplest tactical alarm.

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: White's fourth stone removes Black's last liberty. Once a stone or group has no remaining liberties, it is removed from the board -- that is a {{capture}}.

steps.title: Beyond capture: territory
steps.text: This small example shows the core logic of the game, but weiqi is not only a capture race. The strategic objective is {{territory}}: players try to secure vacant points by surrounding them more solidly than the opponent can invade or reduce. A move that captures nothing immediately can still be strong if it stabilizes a large territorial framework.

steps.title: Preventing infinite repetition: ko
steps.text: The game also needs a rule to prevent immediate infinite repetition. That rule is {{ko}}: after a capture that would allow the opponent to recreate the exact previous board position with one move, that immediate recapture is forbidden. {{ko:Ko}} turns some local fights into timing problems that reach across the whole board, because the blocked player must play elsewhere first.

steps.title: Exercise 1
steps.prompt: Why is a group of connected stones usually stronger than the same number of isolated stones?
steps.answer: Connected stones share {{liberty:liberties}}. That usually makes them harder to capture because the opponent must remove the liberties of the whole group, not each stone separately.

steps.title: Exercise 2
steps.prompt: Why is ko important even though it applies only to a narrow kind of local repetition?
steps.answer: Without {{ko}}, some local captures could repeat forever and stop the game from progressing. Ko forces the fight to break and often links a local struggle to the wider board, because one player must play elsewhere first.

steps.title: What comes next
steps.text: The vocabulary from this lesson -- {{liberty}}, {{atari}}, {{capture}}, {{ko}} -- is exactly what the semantic event layer in the rules kernel recognizes during play. Try it yourself in Capture Go, or continue reading the glossary.
